steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our survey on large language models for generative recommendation. It should motivate the topic, give our generalized definition of IDs and a definition of generative recommendation, outline the survey's sections, and say how it differs from other surveys and what it contributes.

steps.text:

- From multi-stage filtering to generative recommendation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs and recommender systems; the problem of vagueness and the need for IDs
  - LLM profoundly affecting NLP; inspiring other fields, e.g. recommender systems (RS)
  - RS solves information overload, part of daily life; reshaping RS with LLM = promising research issue
  - natural language expressive but vague: vehicle identification and scheduling example ("a black SUV" vs VIN or plate number)
  - RS needs precise, unique item identifiers so recommendations factually exist (hallucination problem)
  - why each user/item gets an ID; but ID usually seen as one discrete token + embedding vector
- Generalized definition of ID

  - example: item_7391 -> \langle item \rangle \langle _ \rangle \langle 73 \rangle \langle 91 \rangle
  - not necessarily numerical: movie title "The Lord of the Rings"; meaningless words "ring epic journey fellowship adventure"
  - conventional IDs = special case, one token; IDs resemble text, fit LLM
- From multi-stage filtering to generative recommendation
  - huge item numbers -> multi-stage filtering: simple methods (rule-based filtering) cut millions to a few hundred, then advanced algorithms
  - advanced algorithms only see a few hundred items
  - LLM can be the single, entire pipeline -> single-stage; applied to all items implicitly
  - definition of generative recommender system: generates recommendations or related content without scoring each candidate one by one
  - in line with AI trend: discriminative (classification, regression) -> generative (ChatGPT)
- Organization of the survey
  - Sec 2 why generative; Sec 3 ID creation retaining collaborative information; Sec 4 formulation of tasks; Sec 5 opportunities; Sec 6 conclusion
- Difference from other surveys and contributions
  - other LLM-based recommendation surveys: we focus on generative recommendation (no discriminative models); taxonomy inspired by recommendation community, not NLP taxonomy
  - contributions: first systematic survey of LLM-based generative recommendation, generalized ID; pragmatic, formulations for tasks; promising directions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLM) are having a profound effect on the field of natural language processing (NLP), and their strong ability to handle all kinds of tasks has also inspired practitioners in other fields, for example recommender systems (RS). RS is an effective way to solve information overload today and it is closely integrated into our daily lives, so how to reshape it effectively with LLM is a promising research issue. But natural language, although it is an expressive medium, can also be vague. For example, if an LLM is used for vehicle identification and scheduling, it would be dangerous to identify a vehicle with a vague description (e.g., "a black SUV") instead of a precise identifier like the vehicle identification number (VIN) or the plate number. In the same way, vagueness can be a problem in recommendation scenarios that need precise and unique identifiers of items, since RS has to guarantee that the things recommended to users factually exist, in order to avoid the hallucination problem. This is also why each user/item in RS is usually assigned an ID. Still, IDs are usually understood in only one form, i.e., most RS research sees each ID as a discrete token that is associated with an embedding vector. In this survey we generalize the definition of ID so that it has a stronger connection with LLM:

An ID in recommender systems is a sequence of tokens that can uniquely identify an entity, such as a user or an item. An ID can take various forms, such as an embedding ID, a sequence of numerical tokens, and a sequence of word tokens (including an item title, a description of the item, or even a complete news article), as long as it can uniquely identify the entity.

For example, a product on an e-commerce platform could be assigned the ID item_7391 and then be represented as a sequence of tokens like \langle item \rangle \langle _ \rangle \langle 73 \rangle \langle 91 \rangle. The ID does not have to be made of numerical tokens. If it is a unique identifier for an item, it can be seen as the item's ID. For instance, the title of the movie "The Lord of the Rings" can be seen as the ID of this movie. The ID can even be a sequence of words without any explicit meaning, e.g., "ring epic journey fellowship adventure". IDs in conventional RS are a special case of this definition, i.e., a sequence of only one token. With this definition, IDs are similar to token sequences in text, and so they fit naturally into the natural language environment and LLM.

Because real-world systems have a huge number of items, traditional RS usually uses a multi-stage filtering paradigm. Simple and efficient methods (e.g., rule-based filtering) are used to reduce the candidate items from millions to a few hundred, and then advanced recommendation algorithms are applied to these items to select a few items to recommend. So the advanced recommendation algorithms are not applied to all items, only to a few hundred of them.

- From multi-stage filtering to generative recommendation
  - multi-stage filtering: simple methods (rule-based filtering) cut millions to a few hundred, then advanced algorithms
  - LLM as single, entire pipeline -> single-stage, all items implicitly
  - definition of generative recommender system: no ranking score per candidate
  - trend from discriminative AI (classification, regression) to generative AI (ChatGPT)
- Organization: Sec 2 why; Sec 3 ID creation; Sec 4 task formulation; Sec 5 opportunities; Sec 6 conclusion
- Difference from other surveys (generative focus, taxonomy from recommendation community)
- Contributions: first systematic survey + generalized ID; formulations as guideline; promising directions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLM) are having a profound effect on the field of natural language processing (NLP), and their strong ability to handle all kinds of tasks has also inspired practitioners in other fields, for example recommender systems (RS). RS is an effective way to solve information overload today and it is closely integrated into our daily lives, so how to reshape it effectively with LLM is a promising research issue. But natural language, although it is an expressive medium, can also be vague. For example, if an LLM is used for vehicle identification and scheduling, it would be dangerous to identify a vehicle with a vague description (e.g., "a black SUV") instead of a precise identifier like the vehicle identification number (VIN) or the plate number. In the same way, vagueness can be a problem in recommendation scenarios that need precise and unique identifiers of items, since RS has to guarantee that the things recommended to users factually exist, in order to avoid the hallucination problem. This is also why each user/item in RS is usually assigned an ID. Still, IDs are usually understood in only one form, i.e., most RS research sees each ID as a discrete token that is associated with an embedding vector. In this survey we generalize the definition of ID so that it has a stronger connection with LLM:

An ID in recommender systems is a sequence of tokens that can uniquely identify an entity, such as a user or an item. An ID can take various forms, such as an embedding ID, a sequence of numerical tokens, and a sequence of word tokens (including an item title, a description of the item, or even a complete news article), as long as it can uniquely identify the entity.

For example, a product on an e-commerce platform could be assigned the ID item_7391 and then be represented as a sequence of tokens like \langle item \rangle \langle _ \rangle \langle 73 \rangle \langle 91 \rangle. The ID does not have to be made of numerical tokens. If it is a unique identifier for an item, it can be seen as the item's ID. For instance, the title of the movie "The Lord of the Rings" can be seen as the ID of this movie. The ID can even be a sequence of words without any explicit meaning, e.g., "ring epic journey fellowship adventure". IDs in conventional RS are a special case of this definition, i.e., a sequence of only one token. With this definition, IDs are similar to token sequences in text, and so they fit naturally into the natural language environment and LLM.

Because real-world systems have a huge number of items, traditional RS usually uses a multi-stage filtering paradigm. Simple and efficient methods (e.g., rule-based filtering) are used to reduce the candidate items from millions to a few hundred, and then advanced recommendation algorithms are applied to these items to select a few items to recommend. So the advanced recommendation algorithms are not applied to all items, only to a few hundred of them.

The generative power of LLM could change the RS paradigm from multi-stage filtering to single-stage filtering. An LLM itself can be the single, entire recommendation pipeline and directly generate the items to recommend, so there is no need for multi-stage filtering. This way, advanced LLM-based recommendation algorithms are applied to all items in the system, but implicitly. We call this process generative recommendation and define it formally as follows:

A generative recommender system directly generates recommendations or recommendation-related content without the need to calculate each candidate's ranking score one by one.

More broadly, this matches the trend in general artificial intelligence (AI) research, which has recently been moving from discriminative AI (such as classification and regression) to generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT).

Using these definitions, in Section 2 we first answer why RS is developing towards generative recommendation. Section 3 reviews ID creation approaches that can keep the collaborative information of IDs in the LLM environment. Section 4 shows how typical recommendation tasks can be done with LLM by giving a general formulation, and Section 5 highlights opportunities in the LLM era. Finally, Section 6 concludes the survey.

Our survey is different from some recent surveys on LLM-based recommendation in two ways: 1) it is organized with generative recommendation as the key focus, and leaves out discriminative recommendation models for clarity; 2) our taxonomy for LLM-based recommendation research is strongly inspired by the recommendation community, and does not just follow the LLM taxonomy from the NLP community.

In summary, this survey makes the following contributions:

- As far as we know, this is the first survey that systematically summarizes research on LLM-based generative recommendation. To separate this topic from traditional RS, we generalized the definition of ID for generative recommendation.

- The survey is pragmatic, because we give the formulation for different LLM-based recommendation tasks when we categorize the relevant research, which can be a useful guideline for future research.

- We discuss important and promising directions for LLM-based generative recommendation research, which may help broaden the scope of this under-explored area.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLM) are profoundly affecting the field of natural language processing (NLP), and their powerful ability to handle various tasks has also inspired new paths for practitioners in other fields, e.g., recommender systems (RS). As an effective means to solve information overload in today's era, RS has been closely integrated into our daily lives, and how to effectively reshape it with LLM is a promising research issue [1]. Although natural language is an expressive medium, it can also be vague. For example, when an LLM is deployed for vehicle identification and scheduling, using vague descriptions (e.g., "a black SUV") to identify a vehicle instead of a precise identifier such as the vehicle identification number (VIN) or plate number would be dangerous. Similarly, vagueness could be a problem in recommendation scenarios that require precise and unique identifiers of items, because RS needs to guarantee that recommendations made for users are things that factually exist, to avoid the hallucination problem [2]. This also explains why an ID is usually assigned to each user/item in RS. Despite that, the current understanding of IDs is usually limited to one form, i.e., most RS research considers each ID as a discrete token associated with an embedding vector. In this survey, we generalize the definition of ID to strengthen its connection with LLM:

An ID in recommender systems is a sequence of tokens that can uniquely identify an entity, such as a user or an item. An ID can take various forms, such as an embedding ID, a sequence of numerical tokens, and a sequence of word tokens (including an item title, a description of the item, or even a complete news article), as long as it can uniquely identify the entity.

For example, a product on an e-commerce platform may be assigned the ID item_7391 and further represented as a sequence of tokens such as \langle item \rangle \langle _ \rangle \langle 73 \rangle \langle 91 \rangle [1,3]. Note that the ID need not consist of numerical tokens. As long as it uniquely identifies an item, it can be considered the item's ID. For instance, the title of the movie "The Lord of the Rings" can be considered this movie's ID. The ID could even be a sequence of words that convey no explicit meaning, e.g., "ring epic journey fellowship adventure" [4]. IDs in conventional RS can be seen as a special case of the above definition, i.e., a sequence of just one token. Under this definition, IDs resemble token sequences as in text and thus naturally fit the natural language environment and LLM.

Due to the huge number of items in real-world systems, traditional RS usually takes the multi-stage filtering paradigm [5]: simple and efficient methods (e.g., rule-based filtering) reduce the number of candidate items from millions to a few hundred, and advanced recommendation algorithms are then applied to these items to further select a few of them for recommendation. As a result, advanced recommendation algorithms are applied not to all items, but only to a few hundred.

The generative power of LLM has the potential to reshape the RS paradigm from multi-stage filtering to single-stage filtering. Specifically, an LLM itself can be the single and entire recommendation pipeline that directly generates the items for recommendation, eliminating the need for multi-stage filtering. In this way, advanced LLM-based recommendation algorithms are applied to all items in the system, but implicitly. We term such a process generative recommendation and formally define it as follows:

A generative recommender system directly generates recommendations or recommendation-related content without the need to calculate each candidate's ranking score one by one.

In a broader sense, this is in line with the trend of general artificial intelligence (AI) research, which has recently been shifting from discriminative AI (such as classification and regression) to generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT).

With the above definitions, we first answer why RS is developing towards generative recommendation in Section 2. In Section 3, we review ID creation approaches that could retain the collaborative information of IDs in the LLM environment. Then, we show how typical recommendation tasks can be performed with LLM by providing a general formulation in Section 4, and highlight opportunities in the LLM era in Section 5. Finally, we conclude our survey in Section 6.

Our survey differs from some recent surveys on LLM-based recommendation [6,7,8,9,10,11,12] in two respects: 1) it is organized with generative recommendation as the key focus, leaving out discriminative recommendation models for clarity; 2) we develop a taxonomy for LLM-based recommendation research strongly inspired by the recommendation community, instead of simply following the LLM taxonomy from the NLP community.

To sum up, this survey makes the following contributions:

- To the best of our knowledge, this is the first survey that systematically summarizes research on LLM-based generative recommendation. To differentiate this topic from traditional RS, we have generalized the definition of ID for generative recommendation.

- This survey is pragmatic, as we provide the formulation for different LLM-based recommendation tasks when categorizing relevant research, which can serve as a useful guideline for future research.

- We discuss important and promising directions to explore for LLM-based generative recommendation research, which may help broaden the scope of this under-explored research area.
